claim: The weakest backgrounds that decrease the gain of retinal output signals are similar to those that increase human behavioral threshold.
source: We find that the weakest backgrounds that decrease the gain of the retinal output signals are similar to those that increase human behavioral threshold, and identify a novel site of gain control in the retinal circuitry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing retinal ganglion cell responses to human behavioral threshold measurements across different background light levels.

claim: A novel site of gain control exists in the retinal circuitry.
source: We find that the weakest backgrounds that decrease the gain of the retinal output signals are similar to those that increase human behavioral threshold, and identify a novel site of gain control in the retinal circuitry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing gain control properties that cannot be explained by previously described mechanisms, and by experiments localizing the site to the AII amacrine cell or its connections.

claim: The gain of retinal signals begins to decrease essentially as soon as background lights are detectable.
source: Thus, surprisingly, the gain of retinal signals begins to decrease essentially as soon as background lights are detectable; under these conditions, gain control does not rely on a highly averaged estimate of the photon count, but instead signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements showing gain changes at backgrounds near 0.02 R*/rod/s, which corresponds to the onset of changes in human behavioral threshold.

claim: Under low background conditions, gain control does not rely on a highly averaged estimate of the photon count.
source: Thus, surprisingly, the gain of retinal signals begins to decrease essentially as soon as background lights are detectable; under these conditions, gain control does not rely on a highly averaged estimate of the photon count, but instead signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rapid gain changes and modeling results indicating that individual photon absorptions must trigger gain changes.

claim: Signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain at low backgrounds.
source: Thus, surprisingly, the gain of retinal signals begins to decrease essentially as soon as background lights are detectable; under these conditions, gain control does not rely on a highly averaged estimate of the photon count, but instead signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on the kinetics of gain changes and modeling showing that the observed gain changes require each absorbed photon to reduce gain.

claim: A rock concert is approximately 10^12 times louder than a just detectable whisper.
source: Sensory systems encode an enormous range of input signals—for example, a rock concert is ∼1012 times louder than a just detectable whisper.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about the dynamic range of human auditory perception.

claim: Visual neurons can experience >1000-fold changes in input a few times a second as the eyes move to explore a typical scene.
source: For example, visual neurons can experience >1000-fold changes in input a few times a second as the eyes move to explore a typical scene (Frazor and Geisler, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Frazor and Geisler, 2006.

claim: Standard cameras fail to capture the full structure of scenes with large dynamic range because they employ a single global gain control in the form of an exposure setting.
source: Standard cameras fail to capture the full structure of such scenes because they employ a single global gain control in the form of an exposure setting, which is often poorly matched to the brightest and dimmest regions of a scene.
evidence: This claim draws from general knowledge about camera technology and its limitations.

claim: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds producing approximately 0.01 isomerized rhodopsin molecules per rod per second.
source: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds producing ∼0.01 isomerized rhodopsin molecules per rod per second (R*/rod/s) (reviewed by Donner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review by Donner, 1992.

claim: At low light levels, rod-mediated signals traverse the retina through the specialized rod bipolar pathway: rods → rod bipolar cells → AII amacrine cells → cone bipolar cells → ganglion cells.
source: At low light levels, rod-mediated signals traverse the retina through the specialized rod bipolar pathway: rods → rod bipolar cells → AII amacrine cells → cone bipolar cells → ganglion cells (Figure 1A; for review see Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001; Field et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews (Bloomfield and Dacheux, 2001; Field et al., 2005) and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The total number of rods that convey the signal increases at each stage of the rod bipolar pathway.
source: The total number of rods that convey the signal increases at each stage of this pathway (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1B showing convergence numbers at each stage.

claim: Fully dark-adapted ganglion cells can generate one or more spikes to flashes producing photon absorptions in only approximately 0.1% of the rods.
source: This convergence, together with amplification of signals by cellular and synaptic mechanisms, permits fully dark-adapted ganglion cells to generate one or more spikes to flashes producing photon absorptions in only ∼0.1% of the rods (Barlow et al., 1971; Mastronarde, 1983; P Ala-Laurila and F Rieke, unpublished).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barlow et al., 1971 and Mastronarde, 1983, as well as unpublished data.

claim: Without gain control, just detectable backgrounds would cause ganglion cell firing rates in excess of 100 spikes per second.
source: Left unchecked, this high gain would cause just detectable backgrounds to produce ganglion cell firing rates in excess of 100 spikes per second.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the measured high gain of the system and the photon absorption rates at detectable backgrounds.

claim: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified within the phototransduction cascade in the rods themselves.
source: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified within the phototransduction cascade in the rods themselves (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000; Dunn and Rieke, 2006), and at the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells (Dunn and Rieke, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000 and Dunn and Rieke, 2006.

claim: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified at the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells.
source: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified within the phototransduction cascade in the rods themselves (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000; Dunn and Rieke, 2006), and at the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells (Dunn and Rieke, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dunn and Rieke, 2008.

claim: On parasol ganglion cells provide information to cortical circuits about subtle changes in contrast.
source: On parasol ganglion cells provide information to cortical circuits about subtle changes in contrast (Kaplan and Shapley, 1982) and receive abundant rod-mediated input at low light levels (Purpura et al., 1988; Field et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaplan and Shapley, 1982.

claim: On parasol ganglion cells receive abundant rod-mediated input at low light levels.
source: On parasol ganglion cells provide information to cortical circuits about subtle changes in contrast (Kaplan and Shapley, 1982) and receive abundant rod-mediated input at low light levels (Purpura et al., 1988; Field et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Purpura et al., 1988 and Field et al., 2009.

claim: On parasol cells are likely to contribute critically to vision at low light levels.
source: Thus, these cells are likely to contribute critically to vision at low light levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the properties of On parasol cells described in the preceding sentences.

claim: The rod bipolar pathway dominates rod-mediated signaling across ganglion cell types at low light levels.
source: This pathway dominates rod-mediated signaling across ganglion cell types at low light levels, and hence should provide shared steps in processing of rod signals.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about retinal circuitry at low light levels.

claim: Changes in the gain of an On parasol cell's spike output are dominated by changes in the cell's excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: Figure 2 indicates the changes in the gain of an On parasol cell's spike output are dominated by changes in the cell's excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 comparing spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs.

claim: Detection thresholds for spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs measured in the same cell were near identical across a range of backgrounds.
source: Detection thresholds for spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs measured in the same cell were near identical across a range of backgrounds (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic inputs to the same stimuli were three to four times smaller than the excitatory inputs.
source: Consistent with the similarity of the spike responses and excitatory inputs, inhibitory synaptic inputs to the same stimuli were three to four times smaller than the excitatory inputs, and hence unlikely to contribute strongly to spike output (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data that was collected but not shown in the figures.

claim: The dependence of gain on background was well described by a modified Weber function.
source: Across the entire range tested, the dependence of gain on background (Figure 3A) was well described by a modified Weber function
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and the fit of Equation 1 to the data.

claim: For the cell in Figure 3A, I0 (the background required to reduce gain by 50%) was 0.076 R*/rod/s.
source: For the cell in Figure 3A, I0 was 0.076 R*/rod/s (marked by the arrowhead); across cells, I0 was 0.08 ± 0.03 R*/rod/s (mean ± SD, n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the cell shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Across cells, I0 was 0.08 ± 0.03 R*/rod/s (mean ± SD, n = 6).
source: For the cell in Figure 3A, I0 was 0.076 R*/rod/s (marked by the arrowhead); across cells, I0 was 0.08 ± 0.03 R*/rod/s (mean ± SD, n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 6 cells.

claim: A small but consistent reduction in gain in darkness relative to its maximal value at backgrounds approximately 0.01 R*/rod/s was observed.
source: We observed a small but consistent reduction in gain in darkness relative to its maximal value at backgrounds ∼0.01 R*/rod/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations across multiple cells.

claim: The reduced gain in darkness was highly dependent on the history of light exposure.
source: The reduced gain in darkness was highly dependent on the history of light exposure, and hence is only partially captured in Figure 3A because we returned to the dark condition after exposure to several backgrounds (see 'Recordings and light stimulation').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations about the dependence of dark gain on light exposure history.

claim: The low dark gain reflects a nonlinear processing step that is engaged in the dark but relieved for backgrounds producing 0.005–0.01 R*/rod/s.
source: The low dark gain reflects a nonlinear processing step that is engaged in the dark but relieved for backgrounds producing 0.005–0.01 R*/rod/s; this nonlinearity and its impact on visual sensitivity is the subject of another study (P Ala-Laurila and F Rieke, unpublished).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is the subject of another unpublished study.

claim: Over a approximately 1000-fold range of backgrounds, gain closely followed Weber law behavior.
source: First, over a ∼1000-fold range of backgrounds gain closely followed Weber law behavior, even though multiple mechanisms contribute to gain control across this range.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Multiple mechanisms contribute to gain control across the range of backgrounds tested.
source: First, over a ∼1000-fold range of backgrounds gain closely followed Weber law behavior, even though multiple mechanisms contribute to gain control across this range.
evidence: This claim is inferred from knowledge of previously described gain control mechanisms and the range of backgrounds tested.

claim: Gain began to decrease for backgrounds near 0.01 or 0.02 R*/rod/s.
source: Second, gain began to decrease for backgrounds near 0.01 or 0.02 R*/rod/s—close to the onset of changes in human behavioral threshold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: Gain scaled inversely with background above 0.3 R*/rod/s.
source: Gain scaled inversely with background above 0.3 R*/rod/s, and more gradually at lower background intensities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Noise changed less than 10-fold over a range of backgrounds that produced an approximately 10,000-fold change in gain.
source: Noise also changed with background, but such changes were modest across those backgrounds near the onset of changes in behavioral threshold (Figure 3B,E); specifically, noise changed <10-fold over a range of backgrounds that produced an ∼10,000-fold change in gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3E.

claim: Noise changes with background were much less than expected from Poisson fluctuations in photon absorption and no changes in gain.
source: These changes in noise with background were much less than expected from Poisson fluctuations in photon absorption and no changes in gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing experimental data to theoretical predictions based on Poisson statistics.

claim: If Poisson fluctuations dominated noise and gain remained constant, the standard deviation of the current should increase as the square root of the background.
source: If Poisson fluctuations dominated noise and gain remained constant, the standard deviation of the current should increase as the square root of the background—that is, with slope 0.5—since the variance of a Poisson process is proportional to the mean.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Poisson statistics.

claim: The largest increases in noise occurred between darkness and backgrounds less than 0.01 R*/rod/s.
source: The largest increases in noise occurred between darkness and backgrounds <0.01 R*/rod/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3E.

claim: The threshold for On parasol responses increased for backgrounds as low as 0.02 R*/rod/s.
source: The threshold for On parasol responses increased for backgrounds as low as 0.02 R*/rod/s, in close correspondence with backgrounds that produce changes in behavioral threshold (Donner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3F, and compared to behavioral data from Donner, 1992.

claim: Threshold increased with a slope less than 1 for backgrounds between 0.02 and 5 R*/rod/s.
source: Threshold increased with a slope <1 for backgrounds between 0.02 and 5 R*/rod/s (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Gain is controlled by mean photon absorption rate and not by the magnitude of the fluctuations about the mean rate.
source: The experiments below, however, indicate that gain at low backgrounds is controlled by the mean photon absorption rate and not by the magnitude of the fluctuations about the mean rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fluctuating background experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Contrast stimuli that substantially increased the variance of a ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs tended to increase, rather than decrease, the gain of the flash response.
source: Instead, contrast stimuli that substantially increased the variance of a ganglion cell's excitatory synaptic inputs tended to increase, rather than decrease, the gain of the flash response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In nine cells, stimuli that increased the standard deviation of the baseline excitatory synaptic inputs by 43 ± 17% (mean ± SD) produced a 18 ± 11% increase in gain.
source: In nine cells, stimuli that increased the standard deviation of the baseline excitatory synaptic inputs by 43 ± 17% (mean ± SD) produced a 18 ± 11% increase in gain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nine cells shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Following an increase in background, gain fell with a time constant of 0.10 ± 0.02 s (mean ± SEM, n = 5).
source: Following an increase in background, gain fell with a time constant of 0.10 ± 0.02 s (mean ± SEM, n = 5); following a decrease in background, gain increased with a time constant of 0.4 ± 0.1 s (n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 5 cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: Following a decrease in background, gain increased with a time constant of 0.4 ± 0.1 s (n = 6).
source: Following an increase in background, gain fell with a time constant of 0.10 ± 0.02 s (mean ± SEM, n = 5); following a decrease in background, gain increased with a time constant of 0.4 ± 0.1 s (n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 6 cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: The decrease in gain at light onset tracked the development of the step response, with apparently little delay due to the gain control mechanism itself.
source: The decrease in gain at light onset tracked the development of the step response, with apparently little delay due to the gain control mechanism itself.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the temporal relationship between the step response and gain changes shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the 0.1 s following an increase in background from 0.02 to 0.08 R*/rod/s, less than 1 in 100 rods absorbs a photon.
source: For example, in the 0.1 s following an increase in background from 0.02 to 0.08 R*/rod/s, <1 in 100 rods absorbs a photon.
evidence: This claim is based on calculation from Poisson statistics given the background intensity and integration time.

claim: The observed gain changes cannot be explained by a mechanism operating on a small collection of rods.
source: Thus, the observed gain changes cannot be explained by a mechanism operating on a small collection of rods; for example, a mechanism operating in single rods would only be engaged in 1 out of 100 rods, and hence could reduce overall gain at most by 1%.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the photon absorption statistics and the observed magnitude of gain changes.

claim: The halving of gain produced by a step in background from 0.02 to 0.08 R*/rod/s requires a mechanism that integrates over at least 50 rods.
source: The halving of gain produced by this step in background requires a mechanism that integrates over at least 50 rods even if a single absorbed photon reduces gain to 0 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed gain changes and modeling shown in Figure 6.

claim: Gain changes transferred completely or near completely for bar widths up to 50 µm.
source: Gain changes transferred completely or near completely for bar widths up to 50 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Near-complete adaptation transfer at 50 µm bar width requires that the receptive field of the adapting mechanism have a diameter of at least 100 µm.
source: Near-complete adaptation transfer at this bar width requires that the receptive field of the adapting mechanism have a diameter of at least 100 µm—so that the mechanism always samples both the bright and dark bars (see Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design and results shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: A receptive field of 100 µm diameter would contain at least 500 rods given the rod density of approximately 0.1/µm².
source: A receptive field of this size would contain at least 500 rods given the rod density of ∼0.1/µm2 (Osterberg, 1935).
evidence: This claim is based on calculation using the receptive field size and rod density from Osterberg, 1935.

claim: Bar widths of 100 µm and larger produced incomplete adaptation transfer.
source: Bar widths of 100 µm and larger produced incomplete adaptation transfer, proving an upper bound on the extent of spatial integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Gain control is mediated by a mechanism that has access to signals from hundreds of rods.
source: The experiments of Figures 7 and 8 indicate that gain control is mediated by a mechanism that has access to signals from hundreds of rods.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the spatial adaptation transfer experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The degree of spatial pooling required for gain control is present only downstream of the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells.
source: This degree of spatial pooling is required to support the rapid kinetics described in Figure 5 and is present only downstream of the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the convergence data shown in Figure 1 and the spatial pooling requirements determined from experiments.

claim: Backgrounds that produced substantial reductions in gain of the rod-mediated signals failed to reduce the gain of the cone-mediated signals.
source: Backgrounds that produced substantial reductions in gain of the rod-mediated signals failed to reduce the gain of the cone-mediated signals (Figure 9B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B-E.

claim: Gain changes do not transfer from the rod pathway to the cone pathway.
source: Thus, gain changes do not transfer from the rod pathway to the cone pathway, indicating that gain is controlled at a site prior to mixing of rod and cone signals in the cone bipolar cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Gain is controlled at a site prior to mixing of rod and cone signals in the cone bipolar cell.
source: Thus, gain changes do not transfer from the rod pathway to the cone pathway, indicating that gain is controlled at a site prior to mixing of rod and cone signals in the cone bipolar cell.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of transfer of gain changes from rod to cone pathways shown in Figure 9.

claim: The lack of transfer from rod to cone pathways, together with the requirement that the gain control mechanism have access to signals from hundreds of rods, makes the AII amacrine cell and/or its gap junction with On cone bipolar cells likely sites.
source: The lack of transfer from rod to cone pathways, together with the requirement that the gain control mechanism have access to signals from hundreds of rods (Figure 8), makes the AII amacrine cell and/or its gap junction with On cone bipolar cells likely sites.
evidence: This claim is inferred from combining the results of the rod-cone transfer experiments (Figure 9) and the spatial pooling experiments (Figure 8).

claim: The region of the TVI curve in which threshold is unaffected by background light has long been associated with the intrinsic noise of the visual system.
source: The region of the TVI curve in which threshold is unaffected by background light has long been associated with the intrinsic noise of the visual system (Fechner, 1860; Barlow, 1956).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical work by Fechner, 1860 and Barlow, 1956.

claim: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds near 0.01 R*/rod/s, similar to the backgrounds (approximately 0.02 R*/rod/s) at which primate ganglion cell thresholds began to increase.
source: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds near 0.01 R*/rod/s, similar to the backgrounds (∼0.02 R*/rod/s) at which primate ganglion cell thresholds began to increase.
evidence: This claim compares behavioral data from the literature to experimental data from this study.

claim: The rate at which spontaneous activation of rhodopsin generates photon-like noise events in primate rods is 0.003–0.004 R*/rod/s.
source: Both of these are considerably higher than the rate at which spontaneous activation of rhodopsin generates photon-like noise events in primate rods (0.003–0.004 R*/rod/s) (GD Field and F Rieke, unpublished).
evidence: This claim is supported by unpublished data from GD Field and F Rieke.

claim: The onset of behavioral and ganglion cell threshold increases are consistent with measures of the total noise (both discrete and continuous) generated by macaque rods.
source: They are, however, consistent with measures of the total noise (i.e., both discrete and continuous) generated by macaque rods (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to data from Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000.

claim: The gain of retinal signals measured via electroretinograms begins to decline only at backgrounds approximately fivefold higher than those that increase behavioral threshold.
source: Consistent with this view, the gain of retinal signals measured via electroretinograms begins to decline only at backgrounds ∼fivefold higher than those that increase behavioral threshold (Frishman et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Frishman et al., 1996.

claim: Behavioral brightness matching experiments show a robust Rose–deVries region.
source: First, behavioral brightness matching experiments, which should be sensitive to changes in neural gain but not noise, show a robust Rose–deVries region (Brown and Rudd, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brown and Rudd, 1998.

claim: The spike responses of toad ganglion cells exhibit an approximately 10-fold range of backgrounds over which the threshold required to reach a criterion spike rate increases in proportion to the square root of the background.
source: Second, the spike responses of toad ganglion cells exhibit an ∼10-fold range of backgrounds over which the threshold required to reach a criterion spike rate increases in proportion to the square root of the background (Donner et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donner et al., 1990.

claim: The region of the ganglion cell TVI curve with slope 0.5 was limited to a narrow range of backgrounds.
source: The region of the ganglion cell TVI curve with slope 0.5 was limited to a narrow range of backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Post-retinal mechanisms contribute substantially to the more extended Rose–deVries region measured in behavioral studies.
source: This suggests that post-retinal mechanisms contribute substantially to the more extended Rose–deVries region measured in behavioral studies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the difference between the retinal measurements and behavioral measurements.

claim: The novel gain control mechanism estimates the mean photon flux rather than its variance.
source: The mechanism estimates the mean photon flux rather than its variance (Figure 4), it is rapid (Figure 5), it has access to signals from hundreds of rods (Figure 8), and it acts on rod-mediated but not cone-mediated signals (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The novel gain control mechanism is rapid.
source: The mechanism estimates the mean photon flux rather than its variance (Figure 4), it is rapid (Figure 5), it has access to signals from hundreds of rods (Figure 8), and it acts on rod-mediated but not cone-mediated signals (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The novel gain control mechanism has access to signals from hundreds of rods.
source: The mechanism estimates the mean photon flux rather than its variance (Figure 4), it is rapid (Figure 5), it has access to signals from hundreds of rods (Figure 8), and it acts on rod-mediated but not cone-mediated signals (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The novel gain control mechanism acts on rod-mediated but not cone-mediated signals.
source: The mechanism estimates the mean photon flux rather than its variance (Figure 4), it is rapid (Figure 5), it has access to signals from hundreds of rods (Figure 8), and it acts on rod-mediated but not cone-mediated signals (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Previously described gain control mechanisms are sensitive to variance.
source: Previously described gain control mechanisms are sensitive to variance (reviewed by Demb, 2008), act at locations with insufficient rod convergence (Dunn et al., 2006; Dunn and Rieke, 2008), or affect cone signals (Dunn et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews and previous studies.

claim: The novel gain control mechanism is located in the AII amacrine cell or the synaptic connections it makes with cone bipolar cells.
source: The constraints above suggest a novel mechanism located in the AII amacrine cell or the synaptic connections it makes with cone bipolar cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the constraints established by the experimental results.

claim: A location of the site of adaptation in the rod bipolar pathway indicates that it should be shared across ganglion cell types.
source: Although we focused on gain changes in the inputs to On parasol ganglion cells, a location of the site of adaptation in the rod bipolar pathway indicates that it should be shared across ganglion cell types.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the circuit architecture of the rod bipolar pathway.

claim: On midget ganglion cells adapted very similarly to On parasol ganglion cells.
source: Consistent with this prediction, On midget ganglion cells adapted very similarly to On parasol ganglion cells (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data that was collected but not shown.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells encode stimuli over 10 log units of background.
source: Considering luminance alone, retinal ganglion cells encode stimuli over 10 log units of background, far exceeding the dynamic range of any single mechanism.
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about the dynamic range of retinal ganglion cells.

claim: In the rod pathway, there are at least three gain control mechanisms engaged across backgrounds.
source: In the rod pathway, there are at least three gain control mechanisms engaged across backgrounds, each matched to the rod convergence at the adapting location.
evidence: This claim is based on the identification of the novel mechanism in this study combined with previously described mechanisms.

claim: Backgrounds producing approximately 10–20 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the phototransduction cascade in primate rods.
source: Backgrounds producing approximately 10–20 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the phototransduction cascade in primate rods (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000.

claim: Backgrounds producing approximately 0.4 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the rod bipolar to AII synapse by reducing the number of releasable vesicles.
source: Backgrounds producing ∼0.4 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the rod bipolar to AII synapse by reducing the number of releasable vesicles (Dunn et al., 2006; Dunn and Rieke, 2008; Oesch and Diamond, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2006; Dunn and Rieke, 2008; and Oesch and Diamond, 2011.

claim: Backgrounds approximately 0.08 R*/rod/s engage a mechanism located downstream of the rod bipolar–AII synapse.
source: And, as shown here, backgrounds ∼0.08 R*/rod/s engage a mechanism located downstream of the rod bipolar–AII synapse; the light levels at which this mechanism is engaged are consistent with backgrounds that are just detectable given the total noise generated by macaque rods (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and comparison to noise measurements from Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000.

claim: At least five separate gain control mechanisms contribute to a single smooth function relating background to gain over more than 5 log units on each axis.
source: At least five separate gain control mechanisms that contribute to a single smooth function relating background to gain over >5 log units on each axis (Figure 3A) suggest that this particular functional form for adaptation was a target of selective pressure in primate evolution.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and knowledge of multiple gain control mechanisms.

claim: The particular functional form for adaptation (Weber law) was a target of selective pressure in primate evolution.
source: At least five separate gain control mechanisms that contribute to a single smooth function relating background to gain over >5 log units on each axis (Figure 3A) suggest that this particular functional form for adaptation was a target of selective pressure in primate evolution.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that multiple mechanisms produce a coordinated functional form.

claim: Retinal gain controls are engaged by each absorbed photon, even when adaptation under these conditions is necessarily noisy.
source: These considerations help explain why retinal gain controls are engaged by each absorbed photon, even when adaptation under these conditions is necessarily noisy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and the functional requirements of the visual system.

claim: All recordings were from On parasol ganglion cells in peripheral primate retina (eccentricity typically >30°).
source: All recordings were from On parasol ganglion cells in peripheral (eccentricity typically >30°; ∼15° to 20° for the experiments of Figure 9) primate retina (Macaca nemestrina, fascicularis, and mulatta).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Retina was obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Regional Primate Center at the University of Washington.
source: Retina was obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Regional Primate Center at the University of Washington.
evidence: This describes the source of the experimental tissue.

claim: The retina was dark adapted for 1 hr while attached to the pigment epithelium.
source: The retina was dark adapted for 1 hr while attached to the pigment epithelium and stored for up to 24 hr in a light-tight container at 32°C in Ames solution equilibrated with 95% O2/5% CO2.
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation methods.

claim: Adaptation at the rod bipolar to AII synapse approaches the sensitivity limit imposed by convergence and integration time.
source: Adaptation at the rod bipolar to AII synapse approaches the sensitivity limit imposed by convergence and integration time (Dunn and Rieke, 2008; see Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dunn and Rieke, 2008 and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A single absorbed photon reduces the gain of the next single photon response at the rod bipolar to AII synapse.
source: That is, a single absorbed photon reduces the gain of the next single photon response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the sensitivity of the adaptation mechanism at the rod bipolar to AII synapse.

claim: Assuming a 0.1 s integration time, a mechanism operating on a pool of 200 rods would have to reduce gain by 40% for each photon absorbed for the gain to be halved at 0.08 R*/rod/s.
